result:
End factory farming.

Not abolish meat. Not ban this or outlaw that. End the system. The one where sentient beings are kept in conditions so brutal that most people can't bring themselves to look, where the law has carved out a special category of "agricultural animal" precisely so what happens to them doesn't have to be called what it is. Where the damage extends well beyond the animals themselves — through antibiotic resistance, through worker exploitation, through land and water wasted on grain to feed animals that could feed people directly, through the steady erosion of our capacity to feel what we already know.

I think about it because the arguments for ending it aren't even controversial once stated plainly. The animals suffer. The workers suffer. The environment suffers. The public health system absorbs the costs. The only reason it persists is that the machinery is too large, too profitable, and too hidden for most people to fully confront.

And underneath all the policy arguments is something simpler, which is that we've built a world that requires people to not look in order to keep eating. And the longer that arrangement lasts, the more it normalizes the habit of not looking — at suffering, at complicity, at the gap between who we are and who we think we are.

If I could change one thing, it would be that. Not because animals matter more than every other issue, but because ending this one thing would mean a society that had finally decided, collectively, that the looking was worth doing. That feels like the kind of shift everything else might be able to build on.
